source.reason: Thermo-Calc equilibrium phase diagram calculation for the Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C steel, providing context for the annealed microstructure.

boundary_and_initial_conditions.value: Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C steel; equilibrium phase fractions of ferrite (α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide calculated for temperatures above 550 °C.

validation_against_experiment.value: Calculated phase fractions show the general trend similar to the XRD-measured volume fractions; the calculated κ-carbide dissolution temperature (about 823 °C) is lower than the experimental dissolution temperature (between 850 and 900 °C). Differences attributed to non-equilibrium state and to calculated atomic fraction vs measured volume fraction.

equation_role.value: Predict equilibrium fractions of ferrite (α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide (κ) versus temperature

model_note.value: Calculated that ferrite forms first during solidification, followed by austenite by peritectic reaction.

unmapped_findings: The κ-carbide dissolution temperature is between 850 °C and 900 °C (higher than the 823 °C calculated by Thermo-Calc); in the 800 °C specimen κ-carbide is still present and detectable by XRD (κ reflections present only in the 700, 800 and 850 °C specimens).

Fracture of the 800 °C specimen occurs by a mixture mode of ductile fracture and quasi-cleavage fracture: the dimpled area is mainly produced by ductile transgranular fracture of γ and the river pattern mainly by quasi-cleavage of α phase; κ-carbide distributed in the matrix and along grain boundaries contributes to cleavage fracture from grain boundaries (large secondary cracks related to the banded microstructure).

The lattice of α phase changes in the range 2.89–2.91 Å, of γ phase in 3.65–3.67 Å, and of κ-carbide in 3.76–3.79 Å; the lattice expansion of α and γ phases contributes to the low density of the steel (6.80 g/cm3, about 13% lower than pure Fe).
No obvious TRIP or TWIP phenomenon is found during the tensile test (based on TEM examination of the deformed microstructure).

Ordering of atoms in α phase or γ phase is not expected during annealing at 700–1200 °C for 1 h (no obvious superlattice spots in SADPs), though ordering may occur during quenching but the time is too short for it to develop well.

For the specimen annealed at 800 °C, the work hardening rate is in the reverse order of annealing temperature relative to the other specimens when true strain is less than about 5% (higher than the ≥900 °C specimens, which contain no obvious κ-carbide in the matrix), but it decreases quickly until failure occurs.
